questions.prompt: Last night at home — did you eat an apple, an orange, or something else? Tell me in one short sentence.
Tell me one short thing you eat or drink in the morning: an egg, an apple, an iced coffee — your choice.
You have an hour free after work today. In one short sentence, what do you want to do in an hour?
questions.context: 퇴근 후 자유 시간 계획 말하기

questions.prompt: Yesterday you got an email from a friend. Say in one short sentence what the email was about.
Your team has a small task this week. In one short sentence, tell me one idea you want to share — an idea, an example, anything of yours.
questions.context: 팀의 작은 업무에 대해 한 가지 아이디어 말하기

reason: 짧은 문장에서도 a/an을 자주 빠뜨리시고, 'an'을 'a'처럼 발음하셔서 오늘은 이 두 가지를 한 문장 안에서 같이 연습해요.

instruction.sentence_length: one short single-clause sentence; add a second short clause only when the learner answers smoothly
instruction.hint_timing: let the learner finish one full attempt first, then give a short hint and ask for one repeat
contexts: 팀의 작은 업무에 대한 아이디어 한 가지

level.reason: 짧은 일상 문장은 만들 수 있지만 관사와 an 발음이 아직 자동화되지 않아 같은 단계에서 정확도를 다듬는 편이 좋습니다.

notes: Articles appear when the learner repeats a corrected sentence, but disappear again in the first spontaneous try (e.g. 'was project architecture meeting').
Compound nouns like 'action plan', 'project meeting' are the weakest spot for a/an — the extra modifier seems to push the article out.
'an' is produced as 'a' even when the learner clearly knows the article is needed, so treat it as a sound issue, not a grammar gap.
Learner leans heavily on 'I want to / I need to / I'm going to'; short answers are fluent, so pushing one extra clause is realistic soon.
